$comment: The system map: the whole prediction pipeline as data. Hand-curated prose, machine-verified structure. Every anchor named here must exist in the code (forward check) and every pipeline step, served endpoint, gate, feature group, performance target and artifact kind the code can enumerate must appear here (reverse check). Both directions run in `make check-system-map` and in the Docs consistency workflow. Layout is part of the contract — lane + column, so a diff shows a moved node. Numbers are never written here: nodes carry binding keys, resolved live from the endpoints in `sources`.

ops_status.label: Ops status
ops_status.note: go-app's own probes: the dataset directory, row counts, the runs on disk.

xi_status.label: XI status
xi_status.note: The loaded run and its manifest, proxied from ml-service's /xi/status. The manifest is read from here rather than from disk, so the map shows the run that is actually serving.

report.label: Evaluation report
report.note: L4's report, proxied from ml-service's /xi/evaluate-report. Absent until `make evaluate` has run, in which case every value from it reads as a dash.

lanes.label: L0 — the events
lanes.note: What happened, stored as it happened.

lanes.label: L1 — the as-of pass
lanes.note: One chronological pass turns events into features that could have been known at the time.

lanes.label: L2 — the models
lanes.note: Two win models, one performance model, one simulator that trains nothing.

lanes.label: L3 — selection
lanes.note: The search that picks an eleven and says why.

lanes.label: L4 — evaluation
lanes.note: Where every choice-facing number comes from.

lanes.label: L5 — runs and publication
lanes.note: Building a model set and publishing one are separate acts.

lanes.label: Serving and surfaces
lanes.note: From the loaded run to the screen.

nodes.label: Cricsheet archive
nodes.summary: Every match this system knows about begins as a file inside a Cricsheet zip — one JSON document per match, downloaded from a fixed list of allowed hosts into a staging directory and unpacked from there. Fetching and extracting are separate steps on purpose: a download can be inspected before it replaces the data the last import read. The archive's sha256 is recorded when it lands, and that is the identity a run later quotes when it says which data it was built from.

bindings.label: Match files in the data directory

nodes.label: Importer
nodes.summary: The importer reads each match file once and writes the rows every later step reads: the match with its teams, venue and date; the eleven players each side picked; and one row per delivery bowled. It also settles identity — a player is keyed by the registry id Cricsheet carries, not by name, because two players can share a name and one player's name can be spelled three ways across a career. Nothing is aggregated here. The importer records what happened, never what it means.

nodes.label: Event store
nodes.summary: The system of record: what happened, ball by ball, in the order it happened. Everything the models read is a function of these tables sorted by date, which is why there is no feature table to keep in step and no precompute pass in front of the models. A delivery row already carries the striker, the bowler, the split of runs, the kind of extra, the kind of dismissal and the fielders involved, so a new feature is a new way of reading these rows rather than a new column in them.

documented_in.section: ### 9.2 Why the event core is enough

nodes.label: Player biographies
nodes.summary: Facts about people the ball-by-ball archive cannot hold: date of birth, batting handedness, bowling style and career end, acquired from Wikidata under CC0 and joined to the player registry through the ESPNcricinfo id that Cricsheet's people register and Wikidata both publish. A backfill writes one row per player -- including the players nothing was found for, because "the source was asked and had nothing" is a measured answer and "nobody has asked" is not. It is a step beside the cadence rather than in it, since a date of birth never changes. No model reads it: X-1a acquires and measures, and a separate gated experiment decides whether any of it becomes a feature.

nodes.label: Venue weather
nodes.summary: Where each ground is and what the air was like on each match day, which the ball-by-ball archive cannot hold: a curated venue -> coordinates table (the geocoder asked about the city Cricsheet names beside the venue, the sides that played there voting for the country and a candidate the top vote out-votes beyond chance refused, 112 rows then placed by hand) and one reduced day of ERA5 readings per venue and match day from Open-Meteo's archive, free for non-commercial use under CC BY 4.0. Cricsheet carries no start times, so a session window is inferred per match from competition and format norms and the rule that placed it is recorded. Both files are tracked in the repository and are the cache, so a fresh clone fetches nothing for history; a day the archive has no readings for is stored as a miss with its reason. No model reads it: X-2 measured four pre-match weather families against the gates and every one is a recorded null.

nodes.label: The rating pass
nodes.summary: One pass over every match in date order. Before a match is scored, the pass reads what each player's record said at that moment and builds the match's rows from it; only afterwards does it fold that match's own events back into the record. The ordering is the whole point — no row can contain anything from a match that had not been played yet, so nothing a model learns is knowledge from the future. The same pass, carried through to today, is the state a live prediction is served from.

documented_in.section: ### L1 — extend the rating pass to emit player-match rows

bindings.label: Retrain due (imports the served run never saw)

children.label: What a player is worth
children.summary: Ten numbers per player per format: how many balls he is expected to face and bowl, how many runs he scores and saves above what an average player would in the same situation, how hard he is to dismiss, how many matches he has played, his Elo rating, and whether he has ever kept wicket. Each is decayed, so recent cricket counts for more, and shrunk toward average, so a player with two innings does not read as the best in the world.

children.label: What job a player does
children.summary: Where in the order he is expected to bat, how often he bats at all, and how his scoring and economy split across the phases of an innings — the powerplay, the middle, the death. A death-overs hitter and an opener are not the same player with different totals, and this is where the difference is written down.

children.label: Sequence rates (measured, not used)
children.summary: Rates over particular balls rather than all of them: scoring after being stuck on dots, the ball after a boundary, the first over of a spell against its later overs. They are computed on every pass and kept in the frame so the question can be re-asked, but the folds found none of them worth a place in the performance model, so none is fed to it. A recorded null, left visible.

nodes.label: The frames
nodes.summary: The pass emits two tables and one serving state. The match frame has one row per match, with both elevens summarised into numbers a model can read. The player-match frame has one row per player per match, with what that player then did attached to it. Both come out of the same code path the live service uses, which is what makes it possible to check that training and serving agree to the last decimal.

children.label: The eleven, as numbers
children.summary: One side's players summed and sliced into a fixed list of quantities — top-six batting strength, tail batting, the wicketkeeper's bat, the five main bowlers, how many bowling options there are, the mean and the weakest link of the Elo ratings — and then the two sides' values differenced. Change one player and these move; change nothing but the ground and they do not.

children.label: Team and venue context
children.summary: The things the selector cannot pick: the two teams' Elo difference, their recent form, their head-to-head record, and how the venue has behaved. They make the displayed probability more accurate and they are deliberately kept out of the selection objective, because a model that credits an eleven for the ground it is playing on cannot be used to choose the eleven.

children.label: Ground and competition level
children.summary: How the ground and the competition score, relative to the format: runs and dismissals per delivery over everything played there before, shrunk toward average, so a first match at a new ground reads as an average ground. Computed on every pass and carried on every row; whether the performance model reads them was decided on the walk-forward folds (gate A-1), because the simulator's remaining error was the level of a quarter's totals, not their spread.

children.label: Age at the match date
children.summary: The one biographical fact the archive cannot hold and Wikidata carries at usable coverage: a date of birth for 85 % of appearances (X-1a). Every player row carries the player's age at the match date and whether a date of birth exists at all; a player without one is his own category, never an imputed age. Whether the performance model reads the two columns, and whether a debutant of known age starts from his age band's debut profile rather than the neutral vector, were decided on the walk-forward folds (gates X-1b-age and X-1b-cold-start).

children.label: What the match was worth
children.summary: Whether a fixture was a knockout or a final, and whether the archive placed it in its competition at all — read from the round and the pool Cricsheet states in its event fields (X-3), which the importer had been discarding. It reaches 96.5 % of matches; a match the archive does not place is its own category rather than an assumed league game. Whether the displayed win probability reads the two columns was decided on the walk-forward folds (gate X-3-stakes). The dead-rubber flag the same derivation produces is not here on purpose: it needs the season's fixture list, which makes it fit to clean a measurement and unfit to be a feature.

children.label: Player-match rows
children.summary: One row per player per match: who he was, what his record said beforehand, what his own side and the opposition looked like, and then what he actually did — runs, balls, wickets, runs conceded, catches. Every player of the eleven gets a row, including the ones who never batted, because who got to bat is decided by how the match went.

nodes.label: Win model — objective
nodes.summary: The model the selector optimises. Every column it reads is a function of the two elevens and nothing else, so the only way to move its answer is to change a player — which is exactly the property a selection objective needs. It is fitted under the contract's signs — a coefficient on a rating the contract marks as good cannot be negative, in either batting order — so replacing a player with a better one can never lower the predicted chance of winning; that is a property of the fit, not a measurement, since FEAT-14. Where a format's version of this model cannot rank results well enough, that format is not offered an optimised selection at all.

bindings.label: Knowing the exact eleven is worth (AUC)

nodes.label: Win model — display
nodes.summary: The probability a person is actually shown. It reads the same eleven columns as the objective plus the context a selector cannot change — team strength, form, head-to-head, venue — which makes it the more accurate forecast and a useless selection objective. Keeping the two apart is why the number on screen can be honest about a match while the number the search maximises stays honest about a choice. It is monotone under the same probe the objective is held to: upgrading a player never lowers the displayed probability, in any format, measured at zero violations per fold. That guarantee was bought, not free -- roughly one upgrade in twenty used to move the number the wrong way, and the one column responsible (the spread of player Elo across an eleven, whose direction is genuinely unknown) was dropped from what this model reads at a cost of about half a point of AUC in ODI and TEST. Since FEAT-14 the objective does not read it either, so the two models read the same eleven columns.

bindings.label: Upgrades that lower the displayed P(win)

nodes.label: Performance model
nodes.summary: What each player is likely to do: runs, balls faced, wickets, runs conceded, catches. It answers with a range — a 10th, a 50th and a 90th percentile — rather than a single number, because a batting score is not a true value plus noise; it is a distribution with a long tail and a lot of mass near zero. Every player in the eleven gets a forecast, including those who will not bat, because who got to bat is decided by how the match went and conditioning on it would be reading the result.

bindings.label: Runs: how often reality lands in the 10–90 range
Runs: how wide that range is
Runs: rank agreement within a match

nodes.label: Match simulator
nodes.summary: The simulator learns nothing. It plays the fixture a couple of thousand times, drawing each batter's runs and balls from the performance model and spending them under the laws of the game — one innings' worth of deliveries, ten wickets, no bowler more than a fifth of the overs. The batting side's innings is drawn first and the bowlers' figures are shares of that same innings, so the scorecard adds up to the total by construction and nothing is rescaled toward a second estimate. Formats with no innings length get no simulated total at all.

documented_in.section: #### The innings sample (P-4 design, written before the code)

bindings.label: Simulated P(win) agrees with the display model
Simulated probability served as the headline

nodes.label: The selector
nodes.summary: The search that picks an eleven. Each side is optimised against the other side's currently chosen eleven rather than against its whole squad, because every feature the objective reads is a property of one complete eleven; the two sides take turns until neither wants to change. Beside each chosen player it reports a marginal value — how much win probability would be lost if that player were swapped for an average one. Where the objective has not shown it can rank a format's results, the selector refuses to optimise, returns the rating-ordered eleven, and every surface says so.

nodes.label: The evaluation harness
nodes.summary: The only place a number that decides something is allowed to come from. It re-fits every model from scratch at a series of past cutoffs and scores each on the matches that followed, so every figure is what the system would have said at the time rather than what it can say now that it has seen the answer. It also scores one locked window that no decision may read. That costs about 54 minutes, which is why it stands beside the pipeline instead of inside it, and why it is run when a number is about to be quoted. Every number it reports is explained by an entry in the metric glossary it serves beside them, so a figure on any surface can say what it means and what to read it against.
nodes.children_note: Each gate below says what it varies, what it holds fixed and what it decides. That prose is not written here — it is read live from the report's own gate registry, so the map cannot describe a gate differently from the code that runs it. The measured value comes from the path the gate itself declares.

nodes.label: Retrain
nodes.summary: One command builds the whole model set: the rating pass over the events, the two win models with their small hyperparameter grid, the performance models, the run's own report and its manifest. It publishes nothing. A retrain that published itself would leave nothing to swap back to, so choosing what serves is a separate act.

nodes.label: Run artifacts
nodes.summary: Every retrain writes one directory: the fitted files, the run's own report, and a manifest naming the dataset it read, the cutoff it honoured, the code it was built from, the hyperparameters it chose and the metrics it measured. The manifest is written last, so a directory without one is a run that did not finish. A set whose arrays are not the arrays this code reads is refused at load, with the run named in the error, rather than served quietly.

nodes.label: Reload
nodes.summary: Points `current` at a run and loads it into the running service. Naming a run is how you go back to an earlier one, which is the reason building and publishing are two steps rather than one. A live prediction made against ratings older than the configured limit is refused rather than answered, because a stale rating is a confident wrong answer.

bindings.label: Formats with a win model loaded
Formats with a performance model loaded

nodes.label: Ops console
nodes.summary: The pipeline as buttons. go-app owns the step registry — which steps exist, what each needs before it can run, and which are optional — runs them as jobs, and streams their progress. The Ops Status tab draws that registry as its own small step graph, which is a control surface: it starts and stops runs. This map is the opposite, and deliberately read-only: it describes the pipeline rather than driving it.

nodes.label: ml-service
nodes.summary: The Python service holding the loaded run. It is handed player ids, a format, two team ids, a venue and a date, and it answers with the elevens, the probability, and either a simulated scorecard or per-player ranges. It computes every feature it needs from its own as-of state — the caller sends no features at all, which is what removes the possibility of two different feature computations disagreeing.

nodes.label: go-app API
nodes.summary: The Go API resolves the things only it knows: which fixture this is, who is available on each side, how big a team is, how many bowlers it needs and whether it must contain a keeper. It sends registry ids and a format across to ml-service and never sends a feature. It also proxies ml-service's status and evaluation report, which is how a browser reads both services through one origin.

nodes.label: Prediction surfaces
nodes.summary: The end of the line: the tabs a person actually reads. The Team Lab shows both elevens, how they were chosen, the probability with its source, and — where the format has an innings length — a scorecard whose lines and extras add up to the total beside them. The evaluation tab shows the harness's report. This system map is a sibling of those tabs and shows the same numbers, because it reads the same two endpoints they do.

nodes.label: Prediction record
nodes.summary: Every answer the API has issued, kept as it was served. A prediction is assembled from four ml-service calls and returned, and until P2-3 that was the end of it: nothing held what was claimed, so when the match was finally imported there was nothing to score against the result. Each successful answer is now written here before it is served — the payload whole, the request beside it, the run and the date it was served from, and the columns a resolver joins on — and the answer names the row that holds it. A refusal writes nothing, because a refusal is not a prediction; a write that fails is named on the answer's `record` block and never costs the caller the prediction. It is not a cache: a row names a rating state the next retrain replaces, so nothing here can be recomputed once it has.

nodes.label: Track record
nodes.summary: The prediction record scored against what happened, computed on every read from the store and the match tables -- no column, no pipeline step, no scheduler, so an import that brings a predicted match moves it to scored by itself. Every stored prediction is in exactly one state (scenario, superseded, unresolved, no result, scored); the scored ones carry Brier and the reliability curve with the base rate beside them, the served 10-90 totals' coverage per innings, and the eleven overlap, every figure with its n. Factored and factorless simulator predictions are never pooled (B-12), the ranges are as served with no day/night adjustment (B-11 is open and the record shows it), and nothing is filtered by outcome: a miss on the record is the record working. It is a diagnostic over tens of predictions, not evidence; the harness's figure sits beside each of its own so a reader sees the record against the number the model was accepted on.

documented_in.section: ### The track record beside the harness

nodes.label: Auction record
nodes.summary: An auction as the operator entered it during a live room (P3-1): the list of players, each still available or sold (to whom, for how much) or unsold, the buyer's own squad and open slots, and the format and grounds it is for. Nothing is fetched -- a live feed is a paid source and is not built -- and nothing here is a prediction, a cache or a forecast of anything, so no row is on the track record and none is ever scored. Beside the record it shows the remaining pool's distribution by role, and the roles are the objective's own two constraint predicates read off the served as-of vectors through one ml-service read, stamped with the run and date that served them: a player answering neither is a batter by elimination, and one the served state has never seen is reported unknown with no role invented for him. A stale registry refuses the role read and every count off it while leaving the list exactly as entered. The module is valuation and projection and never XI-picking: in T20 optimised selection is indistinguishable from rating order (plan 8.8) and the IPL is domestic T20, so nothing here calls the optimiser, shows a win probability or shows a marginal value, and the surface carries that sentence.

nodes.label: Auction projection
nodes.summary: What a candidate is projected to produce in a named eleven, against a named opposition, at the auction's grounds (P3-2). All three are assumptions the operator typed -- at an auction the eleven is a guess, a league has no single opposition, and the venue mix is nobody's fact -- so the first two are held on the record and every answer carries all three back, and a projection against a silently neutral side is refused rather than made. Per ground it shows the candidate's runs, balls faced and runs conceded as L2-B's own quantiles, his wickets as an expectation with P(0)/P(1)/P(2+) and no interval at all, and the eleven's total with him in it from the simulator's draws with his share of their spread. The two intervals are different populations and each names its source: L2-B's quantiles are at nominal coverage on the harness, and the simulator's carries B-11 and B-14 by name. Nothing is widened, narrowed, adjusted for day or night, or hidden, and a mixture over grounds is inverted from the pooled draws rather than averaged from three summaries. A ground moves the answer only through its bat-first rate and sample size -- A-1's scoring-level families were nulled -- and a ground the served state has no matches at is reported neutral. It is valuation and never XI-picking: the Go type it maps the simulator into carries no win probability field at all, nothing computes a marginal value, and no request reaches the optimiser. Nothing it produces is a forecast of a fixture, so nothing is on the track record.
